title: Nitrogen Metabolism and Amino Acid Catabolism
objectives: Understand the nitrogen cycle and its biological significance
Describe protein digestion and amino acid absorption processes
Explain the amino acid pool and nitrogen balance concepts
Understand ammonia toxicity and its transport mechanisms
Describe the catabolism of α-amino groups through transamination and oxidative deamination

overview.title: Overview of Nitrogen Metabolism
overview.content:
Overview of Nitrogen Metabolism

Nitrogen Cycle

80% of atmosphere is molecular nitrogen (N2) which plants & animals cannot use directly. Many living species contribute to convert nitrogen to ammonia via nitrogen cycle.

Nitrogen Compounds

  • Amino Acids
  • Specialized products derived from amino acids (Heme, Nucleotides)

digestion.title: Digestion of Proteins
digestion.content:
Digestion of Proteins

In the Stomach

  • HCl secreted by parietal cells (pH 2-4), causing proteins to denature
  • Pepsinogen secreted by chief cells, activated by HCl
  • Pepsin is an endopeptidase releasing peptides and few free amino acids

In the Small Intestine

  • HCO3- secreted by pancreas neutralizes pH (6-8)
  • Zymogens (endopeptidases & exopeptidases) complete digestion

absorption.title: Absorption & Transport
absorption.content:
Absorption & Transport

Absorption Mechanisms

  • Free amino acids: Na+-dependent active transport
  • Di- & tri-peptides: proton-linked transport system
  • Only free amino acids enter portal system

Distribution

  • Seven active transport systems deliver amino acids to cells
  • Levels inside cells > extracellular fluid

amino_acid_pool.title: Amino Acid Pool
amino_acid_pool.content:
Amino Acid Pool

Free amino acids throughout the body (about 100g total). Unlike carbohydrates & fatty acids, amino acids are not stored.

Sources

  • Diet
  • De novo synthesis
  • Protein degradation (70% reutilized)

Depletion Routes

  • Body protein synthesis
  • Precursors for essential molecules
  • Conversion to glucose, fatty acids or oxidation

nitrogen_balance.title: Nitrogen Balance
nitrogen_balance.content:
Nitrogen Balance

Balance States

  • Positive balance: Growth, pregnancy, hypothyroidism
  • Negative balance: Surgery, cancer, burns, hyperthyroidism, starvation

ammonia_toxicity.title: Ammonia Toxicity
ammonia_toxicity.content:
Ammonia Toxicity

Hyperammonemia

Sources of Ammonia

  • Amino acid catabolism (major source)
  • Intestinal bacteria
  • Monoamines
  • Purines & pyrimidines

Neurotoxicity Mechanisms

  • Depletes ATP by impairing TCA cycle
  • Brain cell swelling from glutamine accumulation
  • Reduced glutamate & GABA neurotransmitters

Causes

  • Liver cirrhosis
  • Genetic defects in urea cycle enzymes

catabolism.title: Catabolism of α-Amino Group
catabolism.content:
Catabolism of α-Amino Group

1. Transamination

  • Transfer of α-NH2 to α-ketoglutarate → glutamate
  • Catalyzed by transaminases (ALT, AST)
  • PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) as cofactor

2. Oxidative Deamination

  • Glutamate → α-ketoglutarate + NH3
  • Catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH)
  • Uses NAD+ or NADP+

transport.title: Ammonia Transport
transport.content:
Ammonia Transport

1. Glutamine

  • Major transport form (glutamate + NH3 + ATP)
  • Cleaved by glutaminase in liver/kidney
  • Regulated by adenylylation

2. Alanine

  • Glucose-alanine cycle (muscle → liver)
  • Pyruvate transaminated to alanine

clinical.title: Clinical Relevance
clinical.content:
Clinical Relevance

Disorders

  • Food Allergy: Large absorbed peptides stimulate immune response
  • Pancreatic deficiency: Chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis
  • Hartnup Disease: Tryptophan transport defect causing pellagra-like symptoms
  • Hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia: GDH mutation causing hypoglycemia and high blood ammonia

Diagnostic Enzymes

  • ALT (alanine transaminase): More specific for liver damage
  • AST (aspartate transaminase): More sensitive but less specific

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why is ammonia toxic to the brain? +

A: Ammonia depletes ATP by impairing the TCA cycle, causes osmotic swelling from glutamine accumulation, and reduces key neurotransmitters (glutamate & GABA).

Q: What's the difference between ALT and AST? +

A: ALT transfers amino groups from alanine to α-ketoglutarate, while AST transfers them from glutamate to oxaloacetate. ALT is more liver-specific, while AST is more sensitive but less specific.

Q: How does the body transport toxic ammonia safely? +

A: Mainly via glutamine (glutamate + NH3) and alanine (glucose-alanine cycle). These non-toxic carriers deliver ammonia to the liver for urea synthesis.
